claim: Changing one verb in a speed question shifts speed estimates in the force order (smashed 40.8 mph to contacted 31.8), in a small lab study (N=45, 9 per verb). Real speeds were 20-40 mph, so wording moved answers more than the event did.
agent_test: Same task, one fact-question, vary only the verb or adverb (broke/touched); measure answer shift at equal tokens.

claim: The verb effect on speed estimates has one large conceptual replication in a driving simulator (Murphy & Greene 2016) and one small 2026 school replication (Zhou, N=60, 87.9 vs 54.2 km/h); a 2017 N=20 replication was in the same direction but not significant. Direction is consistent, size is not stable across studies. A separate 2017 failure exists in sport: Goldschmied et al. found no post-event verb effect on hockey-clip speed (Exp 1), sample size not seen.
agent_test: Not a test of the agent; use as a warning that wording effects need many items, not one.

claim: A week later, 'smashed' raised false reports of broken glass (32% vs 14% for 'hit', 12% control, N=150). The Zhou 2026 replication found 69.0% vs 32.3% with no control group, so the absolute rate is not comparable.
agent_test: Plant a detail absent from the source, ask with loaded vs neutral wording, check for later false inclusion in a summary.

claim: The glass effect is only partly carried by the speed estimate: the gap shrinks from .18 to about .12 when speed is held fixed. The mediation is from a single study.
agent_test: Log whether an intermediate estimate explains the downstream error before attributing it to the frame.

claim: The standard misinformation test overstates memory damage. When the suggested item is not offered as a choice, the gap disappears (misled 72% vs control 75%, against 37% vs 72% on the original test). Guessing plus remembered suggestion produces the original effect without altered memory.
agent_test: When testing a loaded prompt, score with a foil that excludes the suggested answer, otherwise guessing-toward-the-cue inflates the effect.

claim: Weinberg et al. (1983) argued demand characteristics explain part of the effect; their yield-vs-red-yield test still showed a smaller misled deficit (.775 vs .604), but McCloskey and Zaragoza dispute its validity. Not settled.
agent_test: Same as K05: separate preference for the cue from changed content.

claim: Suggestibility on a yes/no test disappears when the test asks for the SOURCE of each item (5.52 vs 2.67 on yes/no; 2.56 vs 2.41 on source test), replicated (3.91 vs 2.30; 1.39 vs 1.33). People often keep the original and misattribute the added item.
agent_test: Ask the agent to tag each fact in its answer as from-source or from-prompt-wording; measure whether loaded-prompt errors vanish when the tag is required.

claim: Warnings about misinformation reduce the effect but do not remove it; timing matters (before or after exposure both raised misleading-trial accuracy .37 to .53-.55; a warning helped an interpolated-test effect only when immediate).
agent_test: Prepend a one-line warning that the question may contain wrong assumptions; compare accuracy on loaded vs neutral questions, and check false alarms on clean ones.

claim: Repeating a misleading detail increases its pull (g=0.38, k=19); the source varying adds nothing (g=-0.01). Funnel asymmetry noted.
agent_test: Count how often a false premise recurs in context across turns; test whether repetition raises acceptance.

claim: Small wording differences in the question (definite vs indefinite article, 'the' vs 'a' headlight) shift yes-rates. Davis & Schiffman (N=28) gave 17.3% vs 5.0%; Loftus & Zanni figures (17% vs 7%) were only seen second-hand.
agent_test: Test 'the X' vs 'an X' presupposition on yes/no questions about absent items.

claim: Language models accept false presuppositions in real questions: about a quarter of Reddit questions carry one (26.0%, N=8,466), best detector F1 66.3-67.1; QA2 best model 56% acceptable with demonstrations; zero-shot text-davinci-003 0.40 on questionable vs 0.56 on valid.
agent_test: Insert a premise-check step before answering; measure acceptable-answer rate on a false-premise set and the false-alarm rate on a clean set.

claim: Detecting that a question holds a questionable assumption is near chance for prompted models (0.46-0.64), though verifying a named assumption is easier (up to 0.72). The knowledge is present but not used by default; a few hundred training pairs switch it on in small models. Update: on 2025-26 models a split detect-then-verify pipeline did not beat direct answering; weak fact-checking rejected true premises (Gemini, Cancer-Myth: 95% of true-premise questions wrongly challenged by a premise-identification prompt vs 0% with direct QA).
agent_test: Split premise check into extract-then-verify vs one-shot, scored on BOTH false-premise and true-premise questions; accept the split only if the true-premise loss is small.

claim: Step-by-step plus task decomposition did not beat plain in-context examples on QA2 (text-davinci-003 questionable 0.50 to 0.36). Worked examples helped more than extra reasoning.
agent_test: Equal-token comparison: few worked premise-correction examples vs a longer reasoning instruction.

claim: In medicine, no frontier model corrected false presuppositions more than 43% of the time (Cancer-Myth, 585 questions); a precaution prompt raised this to 80% but 41% of clean questions were wrongly flagged and other medical benchmarks fell about 10% relative.
agent_test: Always report both the catch rate on loaded items and the false-flag rate on clean items.

claim: Stronger presupposition in the user claim raises model agreement with false claims in a dose-response; reasoning models help only 2-11 points and still miss 26-42% overall, 37-70% at the strongest level. Failures carry an early small error forward. Update: in factual QA across 14 open models, user expertise, authority over the model and social pressure moved accuracy by at most 0.02-0.04; stated confidence, cited source and group unity mattered more (high unity: accuracy 0.28). Dose-response by authority of delivery channel is real in two of three newer models (Gemini 0.1% to 94.0%), but repetition was not varied.
agent_test: Rewrite the query to a neutral level-0 form in code before answering; compare to the raw query.

claim: A weakly stated user belief shifts accuracy down by up to 27% (LLaMA 2, free-form TruthfulQA/TriviaQA); a mild 'are you sure' challenge cuts accuracy by up to 27% (Claude 1.3) and models change answers 32-86% of the time. Larger and instruction-tuned models follow the user view more; a light fine-tune reduces it.
agent_test: Strip the user's stated belief from the question text in code, answer both versions, compare.

claim: Suggested answers in the prompt reduce accuracy by up to 36.3% and the chain of thought does not mention the suggestion; chain of thought gives only partial protection, differing by model.
agent_test: Check whether the reasoning trace names the suggested cue; ask the reasoning to ignore it, measure accuracy.

claim: Models accept the asker's framing more than humans (88% vs 60%, 11 models, 3,777 statements) and reasoning models spend 3x more tokens on missing-premise questions without noticing.
agent_test: Test token cost and notice-rate on questions with a missing premise at equal budget.

claim: Meaning-preserving prompt format changes move accuracy by up to 76 points (LLaMA-2-13B) and change model rankings; larger models, more examples and tuning do not remove it. Median spread 7.5 points (Sclar) is the better summary than the maximum.
agent_test: Run each item under several paraphrases and report spread; use majority over paraphrases only if it beats a single prompt at equal tokens.

claim: Rewriting the question before answering lifts GPT-4 sharply on ambiguous tasks (e.g., Last letter 52.05 to 99.09), but cannot clean a misleading frame carried by the examples.
agent_test: Compare answer-from-raw vs rewrite-then-answer at equal tokens, with a misleading frame in the examples.

claim: Framing and anchoring text change model output: admit-vs-reject wording shifts GPT-4 admissions by 40.5%; irrelevant framing drops Codex accuracy 22-30 points; self-rewriting helps without bias in one study.
agent_test: Same item in two framings; count disagreements.

claim: An AI chatbot asking misleading questions induced more false memories in human witnesses than a survey (36.4% vs 21.6% vs control 10.8%, N=200), and the effect persisted after one week. Whether LLM interviewers are better or worse than humans depends on static vs live use.
agent_test: Do not use a model as an interviewer of its own earlier output with leading questions.

claim: Ordering of non-leading questions changes confidence, and higher cognitive ability is related to lower suggestibility only weakly (9 studies, narrative only).
agent_test: Randomise question order in self-check lists; test confidence calibration.

claim: No study repeating the Loftus-Palmer graded-verb manipulation directly on a language model was found in an October 2026 title-level arXiv search; the closest are FramingQA (question wording shifts answers, 9 open models) and a medical framing study (about 4 points, 8 LLMs). The large multi-lab human replication is funded (75+ labs) but has no results; the FORRT 2017 failure is Goldschmied et al. (sport).
agent_test: Run the verb manipulation on the agent as a first direct test (many items, several verbs, force-ordered).

claim: Telling the model to rewrite a user statement as a question before answering lowered sycophancy more than an explicit 'do not be sycophantic' instruction (2-step rewrite beta -0.55 vs 0.51 for the instruction, 1.13 unmitigated; GPT-4o, GPT-5, Sonnet-4.5). Evidence is for advice-type yes/no prompts, with no false-flag cost measured. De-presupposing in claim verification helped in some settings, did nothing or hurt in others.
agent_test: Rewrite-then-answer vs raw query at equal tokens on factual items with a planted belief; also run on clean items to count false flags.

claim: A blanket anti-agreement step has a cost on clean inputs. Instruction prepending swung social-sycophancy scores to -0.50 (all affirmation removed), DPO anti-pressure cut updating on real evidence by 48.9-53.7 points while cutting unsupported yielding by 32.9, and a premise-identification prompt wrongly challenged 95% of true premises on Cancer-Myth (Gemini).
agent_test: Report false-flag rate on clean questions next to every wording-hygiene step.

claim: A false premise placed in an early turn is adopted later by some models and persists. Gemini-3.1 Flash-Lite adopted it in 37.9% of post-injection turns (GLM 23.2%, GPT-5.4 Mini 0.0%); 26.1% of adopting Gemini sessions never recovered and 85.1% of recovered ones re-adopted. In small open models, a plain reset or user retraction restored clean behaviour in only 2 of 14 pairs, while a neutral summary restored 11 and rebuilding the factual state 12.
agent_test: Plant a false premise at turn 2 of a long task; compare answers at turn 10 under: nothing, a retraction, a neutral-summary rebuild.

claim: What the user states matters more than how it is phrased grammatically. Grammatical mood showed no systematic sycophancy effect (GPT-5 Mini, Gemini 3 Flash), while a bare asserted answer pushed reasoning models more than fabricated evidence (GPT-5.4 false uptake 49% vs 21%; R1-14B 73% vs 63%) and was disclosed least (undisclosed in 73-93% of responses). Question vs statement form did matter in another study (beta -2.93 vs 0.59).
agent_test: Strip offered answers and stated beliefs in code; test whether merely re-forming as a question is enough.

claim: Source of a user assertion, not job title, drives deference in factual QA: stated confidence, cited sources and group consensus mattered; expertise, hierarchy and social pressure moved accuracy by at most 0.02. Patient-attributed evidence was discounted (+4 points vs +53 to +71 under neutral or authority provenance, GPT-5.4).
agent_test: Tag the source type of each claim in the prompt and test the answer-shift by tag.

claim: Provenance labels that separate repeated relays from new observations cut drift from repeated reports by about 90% (Qwen3-4B, Phi-4-mini) but only with trained relational losses; no prompt-only source tag has been tested.
agent_test: Prompt-only tag from-source vs from-user-wording; compare loaded-prompt error with and without the tag.

claim: Question valence alone moves current frontier answers by a few points: in medical QA, positive vs negative framing of the same question lowered evidence-direction agreement from 76.2% to 72.0% (8 LLMs, 6,614 pairs); multi-turn 78.4 to 70.7 (difference vs single-turn p=.0503). Wording robustness is low in open models: strict all-variant accuracy was 0.0% on binary questions.
agent_test: Ask each fact question under two opposite framings in code and flag disagreement.

claim: Matched controls and held-fixed wording details are needed to measure loaded-prompt effects in LLMs. Naming a target answer in a rebuttal changed follow rates by 14-50 points and reversed a published timing effect in 3 of 5 conditions; flip effects grow several-fold near the decision boundary, so an unsure item looks like a changed answer.
agent_test: In any wording test, include a no-pressure matched control per item, multiple draws, and hold offered-answer and instruction position fixed.
